prompt.context: You are in a meeting with the CFO of a large telecom service provider with annual revenues of $67B. The CFO has asked you to develop a program that will reduce costs by $2B a year.
prompt.question: Suggest areas of focus using a structured approach, and identify risks and performance indicators for your cost reduction strategy.

clarifying_info.q: What is the revenue breakdown by segment?
clarifying_info.a: Local Services: $33B (down 1.6%); Long Distance: $2B (up 33%); Information Services: $6B (down 10%); Broadband: $1B (up 35%); Wireless: $25B (up 15%). There are 75–200 different services across those 5 units.
Operating Income = 20% of revenue, down 50% from last year. Operating Expenses = $54B, up 15% from last year.

clarifying_info.q: What is the employee and salary situation?
clarifying_info.a: 203,000 salaried employees (down from 228,000 last year). Weighted average salary = $80,000/year. Expecting a 4% salary increase this year.
External expenditures (part of OE) = $49B. Of that, $37B is direct external expenditures and $12B is capital expenditures. There are about 50,000 suppliers.

clarifying_info.q: What strategies is the company currently pursuing?
clarifying_info.a: Bundling of services; debt reduction program ($53B down to $45B); accelerated broadband deployment; enterprise services growing (1,200 new customers expected this year); focused capital expenditures on growth; geographic focus on US only; cost reduction target of $2B annually.

framework: Identify major cost levers across workforce, external spend, and portfolio
Consolidate suppliers to capture bulk discounts and contract savings
Evaluate outsourcing of non-core functions (call centers, operations, logistics)
Focus resources on growth businesses (Broadband, Long Distance, Wireless) and reduce/divest declining ones (Local Services)
Quantify savings from each lever and compare against the $2B target
Identify risks to service continuity, customer satisfaction, and competitive positioning
Define performance indicators to track cost and service quality

questions.prompt: Which revenue segments are declining and what is the magnitude of those declines?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate absolute revenue loss for declining segments. Local Services ($33B, down 1.6%) and Information Services ($6B, down 10%) are the two declining areas; their absolute dollar losses should be compared to understand where focus is most warranted.

math.setup: Calculate absolute revenue decline for Local Services and Information Services.
math.answer: Local Services loses ~$0.53B; Information Services loses ~$0.60B. Both are roughly equal areas of concern, though Local Services (50% of total revenue) should be the main strategic focus.

questions.prompt: What is the potential headcount cost saving in local services if 10% of unionized technicians are let go?
questions.guidance: The candidate should identify that Local Services employs 60,000 technicians in a union. Since most maintenance and repairs are now handled by computer systems, there is excess labor. Reducing headcount by 10% yields a quantifiable saving to benchmark against the $2B target.

math.setup: 10% of 60,000 technicians released at $80,000 average salary each.
math.answer: $0.48B in savings, representing approximately 24% of the $2B cost reduction target.

questions.prompt: What are the risks associated with reducing the technician workforce in local services?
questions.guidance: Strong answers address service continuity, customer experience, and competitive dynamics. The candidate should also note that reduced field capacity might require a compensating call center, which carries its own start-up, training, and maintenance costs.

questions.prompt: What performance indicators would you recommend to track the cost reduction program?
questions.guidance: Candidate should propose metrics spanning cost efficiency, service quality, and customer satisfaction. Good answers reference both financial tracking and operational/service KPIs.

brainstorming.prompt: What levers are available to reduce costs by $2B annually across a large telecom service provider?

categories.name: Supplier Consolidation
ideas: Bundle purchases across business units to negotiate bulk discounts
Reduce supplier base (from ~50,000) to increase leverage and reduce procurement overhead
Establish long-term contracts with key vendors to lock in pricing
Standardize components/services across units to allow single-supplier agreements

categories.name: Outsourcing
ideas: Outsource call center operations to lower-cost providers
Outsource manufacturing, operations, and logistics functions
Consider shared-services centers for back-office functions

categories.name: Portfolio / Business Focus
ideas: Reduce investment in declining Local Services segment
Evaluate divestiture of local services assets
Accelerate capital redeployment to growth segments (Broadband, Wireless, Long Distance)
Divest or wind down Information Services where declining

categories.name: Workforce
ideas: Reduce union technician headcount in local services (declining need due to automation)
Continue headcount reduction trend (228,000 → 203,000) where justified
Implement voluntary separation programs to limit union friction
Offset reductions with call center investment where service needs require it

categories.name: Capital Expenditure Efficiency
ideas: Focus $12B capex on growth businesses only
Eliminate or defer capex in declining segments
Negotiate better terms on existing capital contracts

recommendation: Focus the $2B cost reduction program primarily on three levers: (1) workforce reduction in local services (targeting ~$0.48B from 10% technician headcount cut), (2) supplier consolidation across the 50,000-supplier base, and (3) outsourcing of non-core operational functions such as call centers
Simultaneously, redirect capital and resources away from declining Local and Information Services toward high-growth Wireless, Broadband, and Long Distance segments
risks: Loss of service quality if field technician capacity falls below customer demand
Customer attrition if service calls are not handled in a timely fashion after headcount cuts
Union resistance to technician reductions, potentially triggering labor action
Start-up and ongoing costs of a replacement call center could offset a portion of headcount savings
Competitor response if service degradation creates switching opportunities
next_steps: Conduct a detailed workforce analysis by function to identify which of the 60,000 technicians are truly redundant given current automation levels
Develop a supplier rationalization plan: audit the 50,000-supplier base and target consolidation to a much smaller strategic set
Model call center costs to determine the net saving after accounting for any customer-service infrastructure needed to compensate for fewer field technicians
Establish a program management office with clear KPI tracking: cost savings vs. target, service call resolution times, customer satisfaction scores, and employee count by segment
